newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka stock market watchdog seeks more teeth.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka stock market watchdog seeks more teeth.

text.p: Sri Lanka's market watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), said on Friday it was seeking more regulatory powers and increased penalties for trading violations such as insider dealing.
"The SEC is building up its own powers," SEC director-general Arittha Wikramanayake told Reuters.
The SEC was seeking more power to investigate trading abuses, regulate public offerings of listed companies and to register a greater variety of market intermediaries, he said.
The commission was also seeking tougher penalties for trading rule violations and wants to double the penalty for insider dealing.

"The new law will double the penalty for insider dealing to a fine of 20 million rupees ($350,800) and/or a 10-year jail term," Wikramanayake said. The penalty now is a fine of 10 million rupees and a five-year jail term.

"A five million rupee fine means nothing if it is a really large transaction," he said. "We thought that the fine should depend on the amount of money made on the deal. We've asked the government to consider giving courts power to impose a penalty equal to the profit made by a person in a transaction."
Wikramanayake said the SEC plans to file in the next week an insider dealing case against the directors of an export manufacturing company which he declined to identify.

"In every market there is insider dealing," Wikramanayake said. "What must be done is to enforce the law and raise the cost of insider dealing. If people know that they'll get caught they'll not do it. Or by raising the cost of doing it you make it not worth their while."
The incidence of insider dealing was now much less than prior to 1992 when there was no regulation before the SEC was set up, he said.
Wikramanayake said he believed the Colombo Stock Exchange, in which 222 corporates are listed, was better regulated than most other bourses in the region.
"We need to close loopholes in the law," he said. "You can't bring in blanket regulations. You have to ensure you do not stifle genuine transactions."

The Colombo bourse, which has been in the doldrums for much of the past two years, picked up in recent weeks and is expected to be buoyed further by the market-friendly 1997 budget the government unveiled this week.
